summary:
Consensual sexual acts between adults are legal in Benin. Article 545 of the Penal Code, in force since 2018, sets an equal age of consent regardless of sex while retaining heavier penalties for an indecent or unnatural act with a minor of the same sex. Legality is not the same as shield: the general indecency provision has been used to prosecute same-sex conduct, and Benin's representative told the 2008 review that no criminal ruling had ever been rendered under the law, on the government's account because families would never allow children to be brought to court.

Two successive codification attempts remained unpassed: Article 88 of the 1996 draft Penal Code would have punished an indecent or unnatural act with a person of the same sex by one to three years' imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 500,000 francs, and was never voted into law, while the October 2008 draft contains no punishment for private consensual same-sex relations and has also not been voted on.

No law in Benin prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics, and there is no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity at all. Legal gender recognition is impossible, so a trans visitor has no recognition pathway to rely on and no statutory protection against being refused service, housing or entry on gender grounds. LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Healthcare is a documented point of exposure. LGBTQI+ persons are routinely refused medical care, including gender-affirming hormone treatment, as well as social services, and healthcare providers also regularly deny general treatment such as malaria treatment to LGBTQ people. The US State Department's 2023 country report records hostility toward the community that is sharper outside major urban areas, which gives visitors an urban/rural split to weigh when planning where to seek care.

Violence risk rests on civilian perpetrators rather than state agents, and on state inaction afterward. The 2023 US assessment describes discrimination as common alongside arbitrary detention, physical and sexual violence and degrading treatment, with violence and anti-gay lynchings mostly committed by civilians while police rarely pursue perpetrators. A 9 April 2024 report frames anti-gay lynchings as commonplace in Benin; neither source supplies counts or a period, so the magnitude of that violence cannot be stated here.

People who report violence or discrimination to police conceal their sexual orientation or gender identity out of fear of mistreatment, and lesbian, bisexual and queer women rarely report to police at all. A trans visitor contemplating a complaint should therefore expect the reporting channel itself to be an outing risk.

Small survivor-support infrastructure does exist. Since about 2020 the Hirondelles Club at the Rehoboth Friendship Centre has run 20 temporary places for LGBT+ youth, and almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed through it, according to the April 2024 account.

Religious institutions carry documented hostility with a specifically trans dimension. Catholic churches bury LGBTQ people in separate cemeteries, priests are documented as calling transgender people demons, and imams, priests and traditional healers perform conversion therapy that families often coerce. Evangelical temples and Muslim mosques participate in homophobic preaching, and homosexuality is publicly framed as unnatural, as a disease brought by white people, and as a Western import.

Partner and family status offers nothing to rely on. The state does not recognise the legal rights of same-sex couples, with one narrow exception: the government grants diplomatic visas and immunity to the same-sex partners of foreign diplomats. Article 104(d) of the Children's Code, Law 2015-08, bars foreign homosexual couples from international adoption.

A small number of statutory protections do exist and should be counted precisely. Article 552 of Law No. 2017-20 on the Digital Code, in force since 2018, punishes incitement through an electronic communications network or computer system to discrimination, hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation by one year's imprisonment and a fine of five million CFA francs, or one penalty only. Article 394 of the same law prohibits processing personal data that reveals sex life or sexual orientation, Article 6 of the 2009 Personal Data Protection Law prohibits collection or processing without express consent, Article 23 of Law No. 2011-26 requires business leaders to prevent, end and punish sexual or sexist conduct based on sex or on real or perceived sexuality, and Decree No. 1999-639 imposes no specific blood-donation restriction on LGBT people. None of these provisions creates a general non-discrimination guarantee or a gender-identity protection.

The government's protective posture is limited on the record. Benin rejected states' recommendations to improve the situation for LGBTQ persons at its 2012 review, with a 4 March 2013 meeting noting that certain things would be rectified. At the 2023 Universal Periodic Review it accepted two of fifteen recommendations, one to investigate and prosecute violence against LGBTQ people and one to combat stigma against HIV. Public assembly by LGBTQ groups is permitted: on 17 May 2013 associations in Cotonou organised a Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia event at the Institut Français that drew 200 people.
tangentialFactors:
The statutory baseline of legality sits on documented pre-colonial practice rather than on recent liberalisation. Anthropologist Patrick Awondo of EHESS Paris has cited evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin alongside Cameroon, Zimbabwe and Burkina Faso, and Melville Herskovits recorded women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom, in present-day Benin; an 8 May 2012 interview with Awondo frames same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a colonial import.

A 31 August 2015 account commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups, covering LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria, describes discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. It is dated 2015 and serves as context for the regional religious-institution hostility, not as current-state evidence.

Stigma in Benin is publicly argued from a cultural-defence framing: homosexuality is described as unnatural, as deviance, and as a disease brought by white people. That framing matters for how a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor is read in public, independent of what the Penal Code says.
localsOnly:
Residents face an employment market that singles out gender-nonconforming people: employers often will not hire those known to be LGBTQ, and the documented pattern singles out transgender and intersex people in particular. No statute bars this, because no law prohibits SOGIESC discrimination.

LGBTQ people are frequently rejected by their families, and families are documented as the party coercing conversion therapy performed by imams, priests and traditional healers. They are also typically denied medical care and social services, even though the government does provide sexual and reproductive healthcare for people who have experienced sexual violence.

Reporting to police carries an outing risk, and the people most likely to face sexual violence, lesbian, bisexual and queer women, are documented as the least likely to report. Police rarely pursue perpetrators of anti-LGBTQ violence.

Organisational life is closed: LGBTI organisations cannot register, though groups can still hold public events, as the 17 May 2013 Cotonou gathering shows. The data-protection provisions in the Digital Code and the 2009 Personal Data Protection Law restrict the collection and processing of sexual-orientation data, and Article 23 of Law No. 2011-26 obliges business leaders to act against conduct based on real or perceived sexuality.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no counts, periods or denominators for anti-LGBTQ violence in Benin. The 2024 report's characterisation of lynchings as commonplace and the 2023 US report's account of common discrimination are attributed framings, and neither supplies a figure that could be compared with the national homicide rate; no trans-specific killing statistic with a denominator is sourced here.

No criminal ruling under the same-sex provisions is documented after Benin's statement to the 2008 review, and no later judicial decision on the general indecency provision as applied to same-sex conduct appears in the inventory. The status of the October 2008 draft Penal Code is unresolved in these sources beyond its not having been voted on.

The claim that legal gender recognition is impossible is stated by two sources without a supporting statute or court decision, and no sources address document or passport gender markers, airport or border screening, entry or visa rules specific to trans travellers, or facilities access. Those questions are not sourced for this record.

The inventory's explicitly trans-specific societal content is narrow: the documented clerical abuse of describing transgender people as demons, and hiring discrimination that singles out transgender and intersex people. It contains no separate finding of tolerance toward transgender people distinct from general LGBTQ stigmatisation, and no survey measuring transgender-specific prevalence within Benin.
